models.title: A plane hides nothing; a globe hides the base
models.mini: The same target seen across water. On a plane, nothing of it is hidden at any distance. On a globe, everything below the grazing ray is behind the planet's surface.
models.text: The same observer and the same distant target, across open water, under two assumptions. On a plane, the line of sight from the eye reaches the target's base at any distance: the hidden height is zero, always. On a globe, the ray that just grazes the water at the horizon carries on and meets the target some height above the water, and everything below that mark is behind the curve. The curvature is drawn far larger than life so the rays separate on screen, and the refracted ray is bent more than the real k = 0.13 for legibility; the real numbers come from true geometry.
models.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: distant targets seen whole, down to the waterline, from an eye near the water.
graze.title: The grazing ray and the hidden height
graze.mini: From your eye, a ray grazes the water at the horizon and carries straight on. At the target it passes some height above the water: that height is what the curve hides.
graze.text: Stand above the water and look at a distant target. The lowest ray that can reach it from your eye touches the water at the horizon, then carries straight on. Beyond the horizon the surface keeps falling away below it, so by the time it reaches the target it stands some height above the water. That height is the hidden height: everything of the target below it is behind the curve. It grows with the distance past the horizon and shrinks as you raise your eye. The heights are greatly exaggerated in the drawing.
graze.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a target's base visible at any distance, whatever the eye height.
flatten.title: Flatten the Earth, and the tower comes back
flatten.mini: The Willis Tower seen from Indiana Dunes, 53 km across Lake Michigan, eye 2 m above the water. On the globe its lowest 180 m are behind the water. Flatten the Earth and it stands whole.
flatten.text: The Willis Tower in Chicago, 447 m from the lake to the roof, seen from the beach at Indiana Dunes, eye 2 m above Lake Michigan, 53 km away [1]. On the globe the grazing ray meets the tower 180 m up, or 155 m with standard refraction (k = 0.13 [2]): the base is behind the water. As the animation takes the curvature to zero, the hidden part shrinks to nothing, and on a plane the whole tower stands on the water. The coloured bands are fixed heights 100 m apart: the tower never shrinks, its lower bands simply come back into view. In between, the surface is a larger sphere, never a stretched drawing, and the side view's exaggeration is printed on it.
flatten.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the Willis Tower seen down to the waterline from 2 m above the lake, 53 km away.
three.title: Three lengths that are not the same thing
three.mini: The drop below your horizontal, the distance to the horizon, and the hidden height are three different quantities. Only the hidden height says how much of a distant target you cannot see.
three.text: Three lengths are often confused. The drop is how far the surface falls away below the horizontal at your feet, d²/2R: the number in every curvature chart. The horizon is where a ray from your eye touches the water; it exists only because your eye is above the surface. The hidden height is measured from the water at the far end up to where that ray arrives. Only the third says what you cannot see. They coincide in one case only: an eye lying on the water, which sees nothing at all. Using the drop instead of the hidden height overstates what the curve should hide. The drawing is schematic.
three.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: targets whose hidden part, measured, is zero, rather than the hidden height computed from the eye height.
canigou.title: The Canigou at sunset, 263 km away
canigou.mini: From Marseille, the Canigou (2,785 m), 263 km away, appears only against the setting Sun. On the globe it stands 29′ below eye level. With the curvature removed it would stand 32′ above: about two solar diameters apart.
canigou.text: From the hills above Marseille, the Canigou, 2,785 m high and 263 km away in the Pyrenees, is seen only when the setting Sun is directly behind it, around 9 February and 1 November; the observation has been recorded since 1808 [2]. The skyline here is swept off the IGN's LiDAR HD terrain model [1], at true angular scale on both axes, so the solar disc is drawn at its real size. The black outline is what the globe leaves above the sea with standard refraction (k = 0.13 [3]); the blue line is the same terrain with the curvature removed. On the globe the massif stands 29′ below eye level; on a plane it would stand 32′ above, about two solar diameters apart. The viewpoint's exact coordinates were never recorded, so the profile is taken from 290 m on the hill above Allauch; a few hundred metres either way changes the skyline by hundredths of a degree.
canigou.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the Canigou's silhouette standing above eye level, at the height the blue line gives.
bord.title: Bordighera from 49 km across the sea: plane, globe, refraction, then the photograph
bord.mini: From 41.6 m near Antibes, Bordighera is 49 km away. A plane shows the town down to the water; the globe hides its lowest 53 m, 41 m with refraction. Xyphophor's photograph, at the camera's own scale and set on the horizon, shows the Villa's roof 10.7 m above the sea.
bord.text: Xyphophor photographed Bordighera, in Italy, from a third-floor balcony near Antibes, 49 km across the sea (Nikon P900, 28 March 2026). The buildings are OpenStreetMap outlines [2], with roofs and ground measured on the 1 m LiDAR of Liguria [3]; the hills come from TINITALY [4]; the eye is at 41.6 m by GPS, over the IGN's LiDAR HD ground [1]. The animation computes the view on a plane, then on a globe of radius 6,371 km, then with standard refraction, k = 0.13 [5]. Then the photograph: its scale comes from the camera's focal length, the same for every model, and its sea line is laid on each model's sea. The roof of Villa Regina Margherita stands 10.7 m above the sea, where the refracted globe predicts 14.9 m, the globe without refraction 2.2 m and the plane 56 m: the refraction of that evening, k ≈ 0.09. A phone's GPS altitude is good to a few metres; each metre moves the measured refraction by 0.011.
bord.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the waterline of Bordighera and the ground floors of Via Romana, 20 to 25 m above the sea, seen from this balcony in clear air.
